query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal treatment that is designed to promote the formation of nanoscale, ductile interphase (complexion) layers along the lamellar boundaries will reduce dislocation pile-ups, thereby alleviating local stress concentrations, mitigating microcrack formation, and improving room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or increasing the overall strength of the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit strong internal interfaces, which under room-temperature tensile loading lead to dislocation pile-ups, local stress concentrations, and catastrophic failure.
generation.intervention: Apply a carefully controlled thermal treatment (or thermomechanical processing) with a specific temperature-time profile to induce the in-situ formation of thin, ductile interphase layers (complexions) along the lamellar boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under uniaxial loading; the thermal treatment should be optimized so that the alloy is subsequently tested under the same mechanical conditions as the untreated material.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, ductile interphase (complexion) layers formed at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The induced ductile interphase layers will serve as dislocation sinks, absorbing or deflecting dislocations that would otherwise pile up at the rigid interfaces. This reduction in local stress concentrations is anticipated to delay crack nucleation and propagation, thereby enhancing ductility without sacrificing, or potentially even increasing, the strength of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy should exhibit a measurable increase in room-temperature tensile ductility (i.e., higher strain-to-failure and/or improved toughness) while maintaining or showing a slight increase in tensile strength compared with the untreated eutectic HEA.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that currently suffers from limited ductility and catastrophic failure due to dislocation pile-ups at internal phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is contingent on achieving a continuous, nanoscale ductile interphase without overaging or coarsening of the lamellar structure. The optimal thermal treatment window and its scalability to industrial processing remain to be precisely defined.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact temperature and time parameters necessary to form a robust, continuous interphase layer that balances ductility and strength. Additionally, the long-term thermal stability and mechanical performance of the modified interface under cyclic loading conditions require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic HEA billet. Subject one set to the proposed optimized thermal treatment aimed at creating ductile interphase layers, while leaving the other set untreated. Characterize both sets using high-resolution TEM and EBSD to detect the formation and continuity of interphase layers. Conduct room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests to compare mechanical properties (tensile strength, strain-to-failure, and crack propagation behavior) of treated versus untreated samples.
measurements: TEM imaging to verify the formation and thickness of ductile interphase layers at lamellar boundaries
Uniaxial tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at fracture
Fractography (e.g., SEM) to assess the presence of microcracks and failure modes
Digital image correlation (DIC) to analyze strain localization during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the thermal treatment does not result in the formation of a continuous, nanoscale ductile interphase at the lamellar boundaries (as verified by TEM), or if the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in ductility (e.g., elongation at fracture) without a reduction in tensile strength compared to untreated samples.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys, such as the 2014 study (PMC4145285), established that casting and modest deformation (e.g., cold rolling) yield a fine dual‐phase lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure which delivers high strength. These studies focused on processing routes that improved overall mechanical properties but did not directly address the inherent limitation of dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries. In later works on related HEAs, researchers have modulated microstructural features (e.g., precipitate formation, phase refinement, colony reorientation) to enhance strength and sometimes ductility. However, the specific challenge of mitigating stress concentrations at the lamellar interfaces as a means to overcome brittle failure has not been directly solved.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved issue is that despite the high strength of the eutectic HEA with dual‐phase lamellar colonies, dislocation pile-ups at the internal phase boundaries during room-temperature tensile deformation continue to trigger local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic failure. No single intervention so far has been shown to re-engineer these interfaces to relieve dislocation accumulation while retaining or boosting strength.
decision.lever: Interface engineering via controlled thermal treatments to induce thin, ductile interphase (complexion) layers along the lamellar boundaries
decision.why: This approach logically follows from the trend of tailoring dual-phase microstructures and directly targets the root cause—dislocation pile-ups at internal interfaces—by modifying the boundaries to become sites for dislocation absorption rather than accumulation. A well‐controlled thermal or thermomechanical treatment could promote the formation of nanoscale, ductile interfacial films, thereby reducing stress concentrations and microcracking while maintaining or even increasing the overall strength of the alloy.
